hook: Two farms grow the same crop on the same kind of soil. One floods its fields from a ditch; the other runs thin tubes along each row and lets water drip onto the roots. At harvest the crops look alike, but the first farm used about twice as much water. Farms use about 70% of the fresh water people take from rivers, lakes and aquifers, so the method matters.

options: A layer of rock or sediment underground that holds and transmits groundwater
The land area that drains into one river
A lake that forms behind a dam
The boundary between fresh and salt water in a river mouth
prereq.why: An aquifer is porous rock or sediment that stores groundwater; a watershed is a drainage area.

prereq.q: A process uses 600 units of input to give 450 units of useful output. What is its efficiency?
prereq.why: Efficiency is output divided by input, times 100: (450 / 600) × 100 = 75%.

prereq.q: What happens to dissolved salts when water evaporates?
prereq.why: Only the water evaporates; salts are left behind.

figure.caption: The crop takes up about the same water under each method, but flood and furrow irrigation apply far more, and the rest is lost. Invented data for practice.

chain.cause: A field is flooded with more water than the crop can use
chain.effect: much of the water evaporates from the surface or soaks below the roots

chain.cause: Irrigation water carries small amounts of dissolved salt and the water evaporates
chain.effect: salt is left behind in the topsoil
roots struggle to take up water, so yields fall

chain.cause: Wells pump an aquifer faster than it recharges
chain.effect: the water table drops and shallow wells go dry

ideas: About 70% of the fresh water people withdraw worldwide goes to agriculture, most of it for irrigation.

Drip is the most efficient (only about 5% of the water lost) and spray comes next (about a quarter or less lost). Flood and furrow are cheap surface methods that lose the most (furrow often about a third). Drip also costs the most to install.
Overirrigation causes waterlogging (roots without oxygen) and salinization (salt left behind when water evaporates).
Pumping groundwater faster than it recharges causes aquifer depletion: a falling water table, a cone of depression around wells, and dry shallow wells.

misconception.wrong: Salinization happens when farmers irrigate with seawater.
misconception.right: Fresh river and well water carries small amounts of dissolved salt. Each time irrigation water evaporates from a field it leaves that salt behind, and over years it builds up in the topsoil.

summary: Irrigation methods differ in how much of the water reaches the roots: flood and furrow are cheap but lose much of it to evaporation and runoff, spray loses less, and drip loses the least but costs the most. Overirrigation causes waterlogging and salinization, and pumping groundwater faster than it recharges depletes aquifers.
